meta.title: Cantonese C1 Advanced
meta.subtitle: 598 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Cantonese → English (see the Cantonese, recall the meaning) and English → Cantonese (see an English meaning, recall the Cantonese). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 598 words for an advanced learner, aligned to C1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand a wide range of demanding, longer texts, and recognise implicit meaning' — a learner here is able to express ideas fluently and spontaneously without much obvious searching for expressions, to use language flexibly and effectively for social, academic and professional purposes, and to produce clear, well-structured, detailed text on complex subjects. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. THIS IS SPOKEN HONG KONG CANTONESE, the language people talk in, not the written Chinese Hong Kong reads and writes, which is close to Mandarin: 佢 for he or she, 喺 for at, 嘢 for a thing, 睇 to look, and the sentence-final particles that carry a Cantonese speaker's tone of voice. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no examination publishes a graded word list for Cantonese, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. All 598 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — philosophy and ethics, thinking and reasoning, academic and scholarly language, government, diplomacy and the constitution, power and social change, the economy and development, organisations and management, medicine, psychology and relationships, law, rights and the courts, the city and its planning, nature and the planet, art, heritage and Chinese opera, belief and religion, the media, language and literature, history, the shades of feeling and judgement, the abstract nouns, verbs and adjectives of formal speech, the four-character expressions educated speakers use, the literary connectors, Hong Kong's institutions, and the expressions of fluent Hong Kong speech: by this level the Hong Kong Cantonese Corpus (recorded conversations and radio, 1997–98), which supplies the commonest words at the levels below, has none left that they have not taught. The cards are dealt by how often the words are heard in that corpus and in Tatoeba's Cantonese sentences, and the words neither has come last. THIS LEVEL IS SHORT of the 1,500 words planned for it: the spoken corpus has no more words that the levels below have not taught, and the rest of the level is the vocabulary written for its topics, so the deck stops where the sources do rather than take words from written Chinese or from a machine's word count. Every headword is printed in the traditional characters Hong Kong uses, with the simplified form beneath where it differs, and in Jyutping, the Linguistic Society of Hong Kong's romanisation, which ends every syllable with its TONE as a digit: 1 high, 2 high rising, 3 mid, 4 low falling, 5 low rising, 6 low — because a Cantonese syllable said on the wrong tone is a different word (si1 poem, si4 time, si6 yes). The Cantonese Jyutping and Tones deck, the first in this collection, teaches the sounds and the six tones. The part of speech is the one the corpus's annotators gave the word, and the classifiers a noun is counted with are taught as words of their own rather than printed on the noun. Example sentences come with 25 of the 598 words, three apiece for 1 of them — Tatoeba's Cantonese is small, so many words have none — with the word picked out in colour, a speaker beside each sentence, and the Jyutping beneath it where every word in the sentence carries a reading the dictionaries confirm. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings: CC-CEDICT (MDBG, CC BY-SA 4.0) and CC-Canto (Pleco, CC BY-SA 3.0). Jyutping: CC-Canto and its Cantonese readings of CC-CEDICT (Pleco, CC BY-SA 3.0), and the Hong Kong Cantonese Corpus. Frequency and parts of speech: the Hong Kong Cantonese Corpus, HKCanCor (Luke Kang Kwong; CC BY 4.0, as distributed with PyCantonese), and Tatoeba. Example sentences and their Jyutping: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
